title: Family Mart joins forces with legendary sumo wrestler Chiyonofuji for new Convenience Wear collection
description: Step into the sumo world with this exclusive convenience store range. Family Mart’s Convenience Wear is a popular way to put an outfit together on a budget, and it’ll soon be getting a distinctly Japanese twist, thanks to a new collaboration that celebrates one of the country’s most famous sumo wrestlers. ▼ The wrestler entering […]
content:
Step into the sumo world with this exclusive convenience store range.

Family Mart’s Convenience Wear is a popular way to put an outfit together on a budget, and it’ll soon be getting a distinctly Japanese twist, thanks to a new collaboration that celebrates one of the country’s most famous sumo wrestlers.

▼ The wrestler entering the ring is Chiyonofuji,  one of sumo’s biggest stars during the Showa era (1926-1989).

Chiyonofuji – real name Mitsugu Akimoto – was the 58th yokozuna, with yokozuna being the highest rank in professional sumo. Known for his powerful physique and extraordinary strength, he dominated the sport during the ’80s, becoming one of its most iconic figures and remaining hugely popular even to this day, decades after his retirement.

Now, Chiyonofuji’s legacy continues in this new Convenience Wear range, which consists of two Line Socks inspired by sumo traditions, and hand towels depicting some of his most memorable moments in the ring.

▼ Chiyonofuji Socks 600 yen (US$4).

These unisex Line Socks feature a design inspired by the shimenawa ropes seen at sumo’s highest-ranked wrestlers’ dohyo ceremonies.

▼ Chiyonofuji’s name also appears in the design.

▼ The socks are specially treated so they have antibacterial and deodorising properties to keep them odour-free.

The socks come in two colourways, white and dark blue, and are available in two sizes: 22–25 centimetres (8.7-9.8 inches) and 25–28 centimetres.

▼ The Chiyonofuji Hand Towel (800 yen) recreates one of the legendary wrestler’s memorable scenes in the ring.

The towel, made in Japan by esteemed towel manufacturer Imabari, is designed to be highly absorbent. Carefully created, it features a jacquard-woven depiction of Chiyonofuji, recreating his appearance in the ring.

▼ The wrestler’s name also appears on the towel.

The collaboration was developed with Hiroyuki Ochiai, the fashion designer and creative director of Convenience Wear, who said the Chiyonofuji design looked just as he remembered seeing the wrestler on television at the time. Ochiai says he hopes that the collaboration provides an opportunity for people in Japan and overseas to learn more about Japanese culture.

The collaboration went on sale at Family Mart stores nationwide from 28 August, with availability and launch times varying slightly between stores. The socks and hand towel will also be available in limited quantities through Family Mart Online from 25 August.

title: Solo travel in Japan: Hidden beer garden in Tokyo is a haven for single visitors
description: This rooftop in Kabukicho is a hidden oasis where all diners will feel welcome.  Japan is well set up for solo travellers, with counter seating at restaurants and private karaoke booths being some of the ways that parties of one can have a good night out while enjoying their own company. content:
This rooftop in Kabukicho is a hidden oasis where all diners will feel welcome. 

Japan is well set up for solo travellers, with counter seating at restaurants and private karaoke booths being some of the ways that parties of one can have a good night out while enjoying their own company. However, there are still some places in Japan that might seem like too high a hurdle for a solo traveller to clear, with one of them being rooftop beer gardens.

Our reporter Yuuichiro Wasai found himself in this position recently, when he was in the mood to visit a beer garden he’d heard about, but wasn’t able to line up free time in his schedule with any of his friends before the end of summer. Rather than miss out on this very quintessential Japanese summertime experience, he decided to bite the bullet and headed up to the beer garden himself.

As soon as he stepped out of the elevator, he started to feel a little anxious at the prospect ahead of him, because beer gardens tend to be a lively, convivial experience usually enjoyed by groups of friends. However, as he looked around, he began to feel more comfortable, as he realised that the place had just the right mix of casual flair and bustling activity that helped him blend into the crowd.

Though he’d feared that his solo beer garden trip might be a hellish experience, this place turned out to be heaven, quite literally, as it’s called “Tenku no Machi – Shinjuku Asia Yokocho”, which is translated into English as “City of Heaven Asian Yokocho“.

▼ “Yokocho” means “alley”

Reaching for a menu before taking a seat, Yuuichiro browsed through dishes like carbonara and churrasco, and an international selection of beers, including Heineken and Zima, all of which didn’t seem to match up with the place’s “Asian Yokocho” moniker, but the options looked delicious so he wasn’t complaining.

The table Yuuichiro was shown to initially had only menus for individual dishes and drinks but he later learned that all-you-can-eat and all-you-can-drink plans are also available. He wasn’t here for a long beer-guzzling feast, though, so he was happy to order individual dishes, and he felt that the venue offered good value considering its location.

▼ One of the biggest draws here is the view.

This building is in Kabukicho, adjacent to the building with the giant Godzilla head, so it’s an exciting place to sit and experience the area from a different angle.

With the streets of Kabukicho stretching out below, Yuuichiro felt like he’d discovered a hidden gem in Tokyo, unknown to the people below. The night view from the rooftop is so impressive that it’s easy to forget you’re dining alone, and although there’s a 330-yen (US$2.06) seating charge – seating charges are pretty much standard for drinking establishments like this one in Japan – Yuuichiro felt it was worth the money.

After ordering a draft beer (780 yen for a medium mug) and a churrasco platter (1,580 yen), his total came to less than 3,000 yen, which he felt was good value.

▼ The beer was cold and refreshing and the food was excellent.

Though he seemed to be the only solo customer in the beer garden, Yuuchiro says he didn’t feel uncomfortable. He didn’t feel like anyone was looking at him either, as the customers around him were either deep in conversation or focused on the night view, so being alone didn’t attract much attention.

▼ The tables are spacious and comfortably separated, so he wasn’t rubbing shoulders with anyone, making him feel like he was in his own VIP section.

▼ He felt so comfortable that he even made another order, this time for a plate of fresh spring rolls (880 yen), so he could enjoy the night view for longer.

With great views, cold beer and good food, this is a place where all diners will feel welcome, whether they’re in a big group of friends or dining alone. Combined with the energy of the city around you, and the sense of openness created by the beer garden itself, this rooftop oasis has just the right vibe to make solo dining an easy hurdle to clear.

title: Janken Kebab: Win at rock-paper-scissors and get extra fillings at this fun Japanese kebab shop
description: Kebabs taste better with a side of janken.  When you think of food in Japan, kebabs probably aren’t the first thing that comes to mind, but there are plenty of kebab shops to be found here. Over in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture, you’ll even find a kebab shop that adds a dash of Japanese culture […]
content:
Kebabs taste better with a side of janken. 

When you think of food in Japan, kebabs probably aren’t the first thing that comes to mind, but there are plenty of kebab shops to be found here. Over in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture, you’ll even find a kebab shop that adds a dash of Japanese culture to every order, in the form of janken, Japan’s version of rock-paper-scissors.

Our reporter Takuya Inaba stumbled upon the unusual setup while visiting Shin-Matsudo Station, when his eye was drawn to a bright blue restaurant called Rose Janken Kebab.

▼ Intrigued by the name, he headed over to try it out.

▼ The sign cleverly uses an image of rock, paper, scissors hands between the words “Rose” and “Kebab”

▼ Stepping inside, Takuya found himself in a cosy little space with two tables and a clean and welcoming interior design.

▼ The menu contained all the usual kebab offerings, with chicken, beef or a mix of the two available.

Takuya ordered a kebab sandwich and was waiting for it to be prepared when the man behind the counter suddenly made him an offer.

▼ “Brother, janken?”

As someone who’s grown up playing janken, Takuya was confident in his rock-paper-scissors prowess, and when the man behind the counter told him he would get extra fillings for free if he won, he became even more determined to win the game.

▼ Janken…

▼ …PON!

With his fingers outstretched in the paper position, Takuya defeated the rock fist thrown by staff, and was able to enjoy extra fillings as his reward.

▼ Sure enough, Takuya’s Mixed Kebab Sandwich (850 yen [$5.35]) was loaded up with extra fillings when he received it.

It was heavy to pick up, and when he took a giant bite, his taste buds were hit with an intense, satisfying meatiness. It was the kind of kebab that makes you feel like you’re getting a proper meal, and he loved every bite of it.

The sauce was particularly good, with a rich sweetness followed by a spicy kick that made him want to keep eating, and the chicken was nice and tender too.

From his experience, kebab shops in Japan tend to use minced meat in its beef offerings, but here, the beef was sliced up in generous portions with a steak-like texture. It made for a hearty sandwich, and Takuya found himself enjoying it far more than he thought he would.

Of course, winning the game of janken added a little something to the deliciousness, but as he got to the end of the meal he couldn’t help but wonder: What would’ve happened if he’d lost the janken battle? He decided to ask the store employee, who replied:

▼ “If you lose, you get a little extra.”

So as it turns out, there are no losers here – if you win the game of janken with staff, you get a load of extra fillings, and if you don’t win, you get a lesser extra amount. The employee also explained that the janken challenge is one of the shop’s signature features, and it helps to add a dash of fun and excitement to every order.

The janken game is less a high stakes affair and more a fun interaction, because while Takuya was eating, a young child came in to order a kebab and the man behind the counter kept playing janken with the child until they finally won, which was a nice insight into the shop’s spirit of generosity.

With tasty kebabs and a fun game on the side, this little store adds a dash of fun and excitement to every order, making it a memorable stop for a bite to eat… and a round of rock-paper-scissors.

title: Is Tokyo’s Odaiba, once one of its trendiest neighborhoods, becoming a ghost town? [Photos]
description: We check to see whether or not the rumors of Odaiba’s death have been greatly exaggerated. Odaiba is a man-made island in Tokyo Bay, but is it also a ghost town? Over the past few years, a number of entertainment complexes and sightseeing attractions in the neighborhood have closed down. ● Oedo Onsen Monogatari hot […]
content:
We check to see whether or not the rumors of Odaiba’s death have been greatly exaggerated.

Odaiba is a man-made island in Tokyo Bay, but is it also a ghost town? Over the past few years, a number of entertainment complexes and sightseeing attractions in the neighborhood have closed down.

● Oedo Onsen Monogatari hot spring bathhouse (closed September 2021)
● Giant Sky Wheel Ferris wheel (closed August 2022)

● Venus Fort shopping center (closed March 2022)

● Megaweb Toyota History Garage (closed December 2021)
● Immersive Fort Tokyo indoor theme park (closed February 2026)

In addition, broadcaster Fuji TV, whose headquarters is located in Odaiba, is still reeling from a 2024 sexual harassment scandal, and has been keeping a lower profile and scaling down fan events hosted at the facility. And while Odaiba shopping center Diver City isn’t closing down, it is just about to lose its full-size Unicorn Gundam statue, which is going to be dismantled at the end of this month.

So yes, the Odaiba district, as well as the Aomi neighborhood it blends into, have lost some points of appeal, and recently many people online have been voicing their opinion that the area’s days as a fun place to spend the day are over. Curious to see if it’s already deserted, we hopped on the train and rode to Tokyo Teleport Station on the Yurikamome Line, Odaiba’s most centrally located rail stop…

…and right away saw a whole lot of people.

Heading up out of the subterranean station, we observed a steady stream of pedestrian traffic heading towards Diver City, plus the shoreline blocks where the Aqua City entertainment complex and Joypolis video game arcade are located.

Looking in the opposite direction, though, things were much less lively.

That there is the empty husk of the building that used to contain Venus Fort, the Megaweb Toyota History Garage, and the Giant Sky Wheel. Actually, it’s also the building that used to contain Immersive Fort Tokyo, as it moved into Venus Fort’s old location. Unfortunately, the concept of an amusement park dedicated to large-scale walk-through immersive mystery and horror experiences turned out to be either too narrow in appeal, too high in operating costs, or some combination of the two, and after opening in March of 2024, Immersive Fort Tokyo failed to make it to its second birthday before permanently shutting down. In the six months since then, there hasn’t been any announcement as to what the building’s fate will be, and even from the outside, you can feel a sense of emptiness while looking at it.

However, while no one, of course, was going into the building, there were a whole lot of people walking past it, and in the opposite direction from those headed to Diver City and Aqua City.

Curious to see where they were headed, we followed the flow and learned that they were on their way to Toyota Arena Tokyo, a new sports and music venue that opened in October of last year.

On this day, up-and-coming boy band Number_i was holding a concert at the arena, which has a maximum capacity of 11,000 visitors. Though it was still some two hours before the group was scheduled to take the stage, fans were already lining up to purchase merchandise being sold at stands set up in the paddock area of the City Circuit Tokyo Bay go-kart track next to the stadium.

Large numbers of fans were also arriving at the nearby Aomi Station and making their way to the arena, making this part of the island feel very lively.

But as we walked back towards the former Venus Fort/Immersive Fort Tokyo building, things started looking very lonely again.

Next to Diver City is a massive parking area, which was almost entirely empty. This isn’t really a reflection on Diver City’s popularity, though, as the shopping center has its own attached parking structure.

This lot is more of a neighborhood overflow parking area, and it’s also sometimes used as an event venue for open-air events like music festivals. On this day, though, it was quiet and still (though it did give us a nice line of sight to Gundam’s head, peeking out from above the tops of the trees between the lot and Diver City).

Continuing down the pedestrian path further away from Diver City, there were so few people around that it started to feel like we’d wandered into a rather nicely landscaped liminal space.

After walking past yet another large and empty parking lot, we were in the vicinity of another Yurikamome Line stop, Tokyo International Cruise Terminal Station, which used to be called Fune-no-kagakukan Station. Why the name change? Because the Museum of Maritime Science, as the Fune no Kagakukan facility was called in English, largely ceased operations in 2011, and its buildings were demolished in 2024 and 2025.

As the station’s new name implies, though, there’s also a terminal for international cruise ships here, which opened in 2020.

We decided to mosey on over and see if there was anything cool inside, like a restaurant row or some souvenir shops.

There was not.

It’s startling how utterly devoid the building’s interior is of anything not related to processing passengers for embarkation and disembarkation. Unless you’re getting on or off a ship, the only reason to spend any time here is to take in the views from the outdoor observation deck, which, admittedly are pretty nice.

The deck doesn’t draw many visitors, though, as it was basically just us and this person who’d brought their SLR camera with them to snap long-distance pictures of the boats in the bay.

Speaking of boats, though the Museum of Maritime Science is no more, its biggest attraction is still on display. Even after the museum’s closure, the Soya icebreaker vessel, famous for a series of Antarctic research and rescue missions in the 1950s and ‘60s, remains docked in Odaiba as a museum ship.

As you can see, though, it wasn’t exactly buzzing with activity, and that was sort of the theme for the rest of our walk around Odaiba.

At one point, we came across this group of perched pigeons lined up on top of a fence, and it was more company than we’d had for a long time. As if to hammer home the point that this wasn’t really a people place, not a single one of the birds felt the need to fly off or otherwise put any distance between us as we walked by.

Once we were back to Tokyo Teleport Station, though, we had many members of our own species around us, a lot of them walking towards Toyota Arena Tokyo as the start time for Number_i’s concert drew nearer.

So can Odaiba be called a ghost town? Eh, that’d be going too far. It’s definitely lost a lot of the energy it had during the early 2000s, when it enjoyed a reputation as a fashionably trendy part of town. In particular, the losses of Oedo Onsen Monogatari and Venus Fort took a lot of the buzzing excitement with them, since there were both adjacent to the plaza in front of Tokyo Teleport Station. Instead of having a lively central hub, visitors to the neighborhood are now funneled off in different directions to venues several blocks away from each other, so there isn’t the same cohesive fun atmosphere there used to be.

That said, once you get closer to those currently active venues, the mood brightens up considerably. However, the drawing power of Toyota Arena Tokyo is going to vary significantly depending on whether or not there’s an event going on that day, as well as by what the event is. Also, while the Tokyo Big Sight convention center is technically in the Ariake district that’s across a canal from Odaiba/Aomi, major events held there can also draw more people to Odaiba, since it offers more dining/shopping options than Ariake does, but again, it doesn’t have things going on seven days a week.

So it’s still too early to write Odaiba off, but it does seem like its visitor numbers are going to fluctuate more than they did in the past, especially with the upcoming loss of another every-day attraction when the Unicorn Gundam is removed.

title: Family Mart releases new Human Made Cup Noodle in Japan, with freebies for Nigo fans
description: Japanese convenience store essential gets a cool Human Made makeover. content:
Japanese convenience store essential gets a cool Human Made makeover.

Ever since Family Mart opened a new “Famima” flagship store in Tokyo last month, the convenience store chain has been undergoing something of a transformation, leaning heavily into street culture through its collaboration with Nigo, the founder of streetwear brand Bape and lifestyle brand Human Made.

After releasing a whole slew of stylish new goods at branches nationwide, Family Mart is now forging ties with Nigo once again, this time for an exclusive new Cup Noodle that bears the name “Human Made”.

▼ Despite the name, the “Human Made” noodles are regular Cup Noodle flavour.

Fans of the brand will love all the nods to Human Made in this Cup Noodle, starting with the distinctive heart logo, which usually appears with three diagonal stripes on the upper right. For this collaboration, those stripes are given a wavy twist to resemble Nissin’s instant noodles, with the heart appearing behind the words “Human Made”, printed in the distinctive Cup Noodle font.

▼ Nissin and Human Made logos appear around the lid’s opening tab as well.

The real showstopper lies beneath the lid, because when you lift it up, you’ll be met by Human Made’s iconic polar bear graphic.

▼ The pull tabs on the lid sit perfectly with the design to mimic the ears of a polar bear.

While the cute details alone are enough reason to want one of these, there’s even more incentive to buy as the chain is running a campaign to mark the release. Customers who purchase one limited-edition Human Made Cup Noodle will receive one of three Human Made items: one of two sticker designs or an A4-size clear file.

▼ Human Made stickers, available in two designs.

▼ A4-size Human Made clear file.

Buy two Cup Noodle Human Made products and you’ll receive one of two larger items: a fork or an eco bag.

▼ Human Made fork

▼ Human Made eco bag

The campaign runs from 10 a.m. on 1 September until 14 September, and the promotional gifts are only available while supplies last. The limited-edition Cup Noodle will retail for 248 yen (US$1.67), and can be purchased at Family Mart stores across Japan from 1 September.

title: This Japanese 7-Eleven has the most expensive drinks, and item, we’ve even seen at the chain
description: But the startlingly pricy item isn’t something that you can eat or drink. When international travel fans hear the name Niseko, they think of some of the finest skiing and snowboarding venues that Japan has to offer. For many Japanese residents, though, the first thing that springs to mind when they think of this town […]
content:
But the startlingly pricy item isn’t something that you can eat or drink.

When international travel fans hear the name Niseko, they think of some of the finest skiing and snowboarding venues that Japan has to offer. For many Japanese residents, though, the first thing that springs to mind when they think of this town in Hokkaido Prefecture is high prices.

Because of the weak yen, Japan is not only receiving more international visitors than ever before, they’re spending more as well. Factor in the fact that winter sports already tend to be a wealthy person’s hobby, and it creates a situation where there’s a lot of foreign tourist money chasing goods and services in Niseko these days. There are residual effects on prices even in the non-snowy season, during which the town is also seeing more overseas tourists than it did before as it increasingly features in travel roundups of must-visit places on a trip to Japan.

But even with that backdrop, we were still shocked at the luxury we found for sale in a Niseko 7-Ekeven.

We stopped by Niseko on a recent trip to Hokkaido (after trying Ainu cuisine elsewhere in the prefecture). While there’s obviously no skiing or snowboarding to be done at this time of year, there’s plenty of beautiful mountain and forest scenery, plus outdoor activities such as river rafting and ziplining, that can be enjoyed in the town’s “green season.”

Niseko Village, a collection of shops and restaurants, is also open during the summer, although with some tenants taking time off until the snow starts falling again.

Taking a look at the menu boards of the restaurants that were open, we spotted several examples of the infamous “Niseko kakaku,” or “Niseko prices.”

For example, Ramen Dining Gogyo is a restaurant managed by Ippudo, a ramen chain founded in Fukuoka Prefecture, that sells its specialty tonkotsu ramen for around 1,000 yen (US$6.30) a bowl. At Gogyo, though, they charge roughly double that, 1,980 yen.

Those prices still might not sound so bad if you’re converting them to a foreign currency, but for locals who get paid in yen, they’re astronomical. The modestly sized “artisan pizzas” being offered at another restaurant in the village weren’t any more wallet-friendly, starting at 3,300 yen.

▼ Another tell-tale sign of tourist-oriented menu design: the presence of pepperoni, which isn’t a particularly popular topping at Japanese pizza places.

And while it’s not located in the Niseko Village center, the Niseko Branch of 7-Eleven gave us the biggest shocks of the day.

Thankfully, there weren’t any opportunistic markups here, as Japanese convenience store chains are pretty strict on keeping prices more or less uniform across the country. Because of that, at first, as we browsed the aisles, this 7-Eleven looked, and was priced like, any other in Japan.

But then we got to the liquor section, and in addition to regular, affordable things like cans of Asahi Super Dry and Kirin Hyoketsu, we discovered far more high-end spirits than the typical 7-Eleven has on its shelves, like the whiskies shown in this photo which were priced at 8,800, 9,900, and 9,680 yen.

Still not fancy enough? No problem, because this 7-Eleven is also stocked with Suntory’s 12-year Yamazaki, for 55,000 yen a bottle.

▼ There are studio apartments in Japan that don’t charge this much for a month’s rent.

Not into brown liquors? Maybe a 5,192-yen bottle of craft gin is something you’d like to toss in your basket along with your Pocky and melon bread on your convenience store run.

Or, if you’re craving something bubbly, you could pick up a 27,500-yen bottle of champagne.

▼ The 7-Eleven logo and a five-digit number are a wild combination to see on a price sticker.

This lineup is pretty clearly aimed at deep-pocketed travelers from overseas, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re buying it. However, when we asked the clerk “Do you actually sell much of these expensive liquors?” they told us:

“Hahaha yeah, we sell a whole lot of it.”

As we’d expected, the clerk told us the primary buyers of the pricey booze are international tourists, saying that they nonchalantly pick out bottles without much more gravitas to the purchase than someone doing their regular grocery shopping.

And yet, the craziest, and most crazily priced, item we saw in this Niseko 7-Eleven wasn’t a bottle.

It was a vase.

Sitting nonchalantly in a corner of the store with local tourism pamphlets and a poster touting “Souvenir of Japan, one-of-a-kind” was a large ceramic vase, with a very large price tag.

Yep, that’s a 500,000-yen (US$3.150) souvenir for sale in a 7-Eleven.

To be fair, this might actually be a bargain price. We’re not fine art appraisers here at SoraNews24 (our expertise hews closer to things like Sanrio artifacts), and the vase looked like it’s probably an antique, so we’re not saying the 500,000-yen price is out of line, just entirely outside the sort of thing you expect to see in a convenience store, and one more example of how Niseko is sort of an economy unto itself these days.

title: Mister Donut releases new doughnuts that look and taste like Japanese sweet potatoes
description: Limited-edition collection serves up a taste of Japanese autumn with deliciously clever details. Mister Donut is celebrating the arrival of autumn with five doughnuts inspired by one of Japan’s favourite seasonal ingredients: sweet potatoes. Called “Satsumaimo Do”, this new collection features five varieties, each designed to capture the flavour and texture of Japanese sweet potatoes […]
content:
Limited-edition collection serves up a taste of Japanese autumn with deliciously clever details.

Mister Donut is celebrating the arrival of autumn with five doughnuts inspired by one of Japan’s favourite seasonal ingredients: sweet potatoes. Called “Satsumaimo Do”, this new collection features five varieties, each designed to capture the flavour and texture of Japanese sweet potatoes in a different way.

▼ “Satsumaimo Do” combines the Japanese word for sweet potato (“satsumaimo”) with “do” (short for “doughnut”).

Sweet potato doughnuts are a popular seasonal offering at Mister Donut, but this year they’ve been given a new shape and thicker dough to make them look and feel even more like sweet potatoes. The shape is designed to resemble three small sweet potatoes joined together, made with a dough that contains 1.3 percent sweet potato powder for a delicious flavour and a soft, fluffy mouthfeel.

▼ Satsumaimo Do Plain (183 yen [US$1.15] for takeout; 187 yen dine-in)

The simplest of the five, this doughnut lets the sweet potato dough take centre stage, so you can fully enjoy the flavour and soft texture.

▼ Satsumaimo Do Stone-Roasted Sweet Potato-style (194 yen takeout; 198 yen dine-in)

This three-lobed doughnut is coated in a glaze that makes it look like three Japanese stone-roasted sweet potatoes, complete with a roasted sweetness to mimic the distinctive flavour.

▼ Satsumaimo Do Melty Salted Butter (194 yen takeout; 198 yen dine-in)

A lightly salted butter sauce and iced sugar coating gives this doughnut a delectably soft, gooey texture that adds a savoury-sweet contrast to the dough.

▼ Satsumaimo Do Fragrant Creme Brulee (216 yen takeout; 220 yen dine-in)

This version is topped with a layer of rich egg-based cream and finished with a crispy brulee sheet, creating a fantastic combination of creamy, crunchy and soft textures.

▼ Satsumaimo Do Rich Sweet Potato (216 yen takeout; 198 yen dine-in)

This beauty is filled with a rich sweet potato filling containing fresh cream, then baked in the oven to give the top a fragrant, roasted finish.

The Satsumaimo Do collection will be available at Mister Donut stores across Japan from 2 September, while stocks last.

title: Mos Burger skips tsukimi burgers, crafts moon-viewing focaccia sausage sandwiches instead
description: Newest entry in the chain’s tsukimi burger alternative features a rich and creamy “Golden Sauce.” Autumn is the season for tsukimi (moon-viewing) in Japan, which also makes it the season for tsukimi burgers, hamburgers topped with an egg reminiscent of the full moon. So you might assume that Mos Burger, Japan’s most popular home-grown burger […]
content:
Newest entry in the chain’s tsukimi burger alternative features a rich and creamy “Golden Sauce.”

Autumn is the season for tsukimi (moon-viewing) in Japan, which also makes it the season for tsukimi burgers, hamburgers topped with an egg reminiscent of the full moon. So you might assume that Mos Burger, Japan’s most popular home-grown burger chain, is set to add tsukimi burgers of its own to its menu for the next several weeks.

In actuality, though, Mos Burger traditionally lets other Japanese fast food chains duke it out in the crowded tsukimi burger field and offers something different instead: tsukimi focaccia sausage sandwiches, and this year it’s bringing out a new version.

The Tsukimi Focaccia Golden Cheese Sauce (or Ogon Cheese Sauce, if you’re ordering it in Japanese) keeps the thick focaccia fold-over bun and smokey semicircle sausage that are the customary elements of Mos Burger’s tsukimi series. For your veggies, you get shredded cabbage and minced onions, and fulfilling the tsukimi qualification here is a melty soft-boiled egg, but it’s not the only eggy element. The Golden Cheese Sauce is a black pepper-accented mixture of Parmesan and cheddar cheeses plus powdered egg yolk. The result, Mos promises, is rich and creamy while still blending harmoniously with the other ingredients for a decadently satisfying sandwich.

As a matter of fact, if the sauce is sounding so tasty to you that you don’t even need the tsukimi-ness, Mos Burger can also make you a Golden Cheese Sauce Focaccia with no soft-boiled egg (though it still has the powdered egg yolk in the sauce).

The tsukimi version of the sandwich is priced at 630 yen (US$4), and its simpler counterpart at 560 yen. Both go on sale September 9 and are scheduled to be available through early November. And if tsukimi focaccia has you wondering what other foods the concept could be applied to, Pizza Hut Japan’s ovens will soon be cooking tsukimi sukiyaki pizzas.

title: Studio Ghibli unveils new anime calendars and diary planners for 2027
description: Schedule your days the Ghibli way, with a dash of magic on every page of the year. With the end of the year now fast approaching, 2027 diaries and calendars are beginning to pop up on the market, and some of the sweetest come from Studio Ghibli. content:
Schedule your days the Ghibli way, with a dash of magic on every page of the year.

With the end of the year now fast approaching, 2027 diaries and calendars are beginning to pop up on the market, and some of the sweetest come from Studio Ghibli. This time, there are four planners and two calendars to choose from, all featuring beloved characters and movie scenes that’ll make you smile all year long.

▼ The journey to 2027 begins with four planners, priced at 2,090 yen (US$13.15) each.

▼ My Neighbour Totoro 

All the planners (which are listed as both “schedule books” and “diaries”) come with faux leather covers that are smooth and pleasant to touch. Both the front and back of the covers are adorned in shiny details that capture the mood of the film they honour, with an action-packed scene on the front, and a more contemplative, quiet scene on the rear.

The Totoro planner recalls the nighttime scene from the film, showing all three Totoros – Large, Medium and Small – flying through the sky on a giant spinning top, with Mei and Satsuki along for the ride. On the back, we see Satsuki and Mei’s father at his desk, gazing upward as if he might be catching a glimpse of them.

▼ The journey continues inside, with an opening page that sets the scene with an establishing shot, which in this case shows the countryside home where Satsuki and Mei live with their father.

Turn the page and you’ll find a variety of handy planner-friendly sections, including year-at-a-glance pages…

▼ … monthly pages…

▼ …and weekly pages, all adorned with cute motifs from the film.

▼ There are beautiful sections for note-taking as well, with lined and graph pages…

▼ …an address and personal information section…

▼ … and a variety of memo cards, which can be cut out and shared with friends.

Each planner is B6-sized (19 × 13.5 × 10 centimetres [7.48 × 5.31 × 3.94 inches]) and contains 128 pages, making them easy to use at home, in the office or on the go.

▼ Spirited Away

The Spirited Away scheduler takes us to the home of Zeniba, where protagonist Chihiro travels to with Boh Mouse, Yu-Bird in fly form and No Face, before hitching a ride back to the bathhouse on dragon Haku.

▼ Motifs from the film add a dash of Ghibli magic to every day of the year.

▼ Yubaba will be keeping her steely gaze on you in the notes section…

▼…while No Face will soothe your soul with a gentle knitting scene from Zeniba’s house.

▼ Channel Chihiro and Haku with your personal memo section…

▼ …and the memo cards are so cute you’ll want to keep them all to yourself.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service

The cover features Kiki on her broomstick with Jiji, recalling the scene where they’re joined by wild geese while making her stuffed toy delivery, moments before they all get blown off course.

▼ The stuffed toy, which happens to look just like Jiji, winds up lost in the process, with Kiki eventually finding it in the windowsill of a hut in the woods.

This is when Kiki meets Ursula, who lives in the hut, and the beginning of their close friendship is captured on the first page of the diary.

▼ This sweet image recalls the scene where Kiki climbs to the roof of the hut to find Ursula sketching the crows.

Motifs from the film, and the bakery that features in it, adorn the pages like little Easter eggs just waiting to be found.

The personal notes and memo section takes you from the blissful idyll of Kiki’s childhood home through to the seaside bakery, where her delivery adventures begin.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle

Soar above the rooftops with Howl and Sophie in this beautiful gold-on-pink design, with nods to some of their magical companions on the back.

▼ The movie characters and setting welcome you to explore every day of the year from the very first page.

▼ Fun fact: the anime town is inspired by real-world Colmar in northeastern France.

Howl and Sophie’s love story spreads out across the pages of the diary, with a little help from the supporting cast.


▼ Calcifer and Heen make an appearance.

▼ As does the castle, itself, which is a character in its own right.

▼ With so many beautiful images within its pages, this is a diary you’ll be reaching for time and time again.


If you prefer to have Ghibli anime art readily visible in a more prominent way, you can opt for one of two Studio Ghibli calendars.

▼ 2027 Studio Ghibli Art Frame Calendar (3,300 yen)

The art calendar is a popular choice for fans, as it comes in two parts, with the artwork supplied as separate sheets to be inserted between a transparent cover and frame mat in the upper section of the calendar.

▼ These instructions show how one sheet of art at a time can be inserted into the display section at the top of the calendar.

Images from 23 Ghibli feature films are included in the set, giving you the chance to display around two films a month if you wanted to, although the choice of when to display them is entirely up to you. Some of the films include:

▼ Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (technically created before the founding of Studio Ghibli, but counted as a Ghibli film in this collection)

▼ Spirited Away

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle

Even after the year is over, you can easily frame your favourite images so you can have a framed Ghibli work on your wall for years to come.

▼ My Neighbor Totoro Calendar (1,980 yen)

The final product in the 2027 lineup is a calendar dedicated to My Neighbour Totoro, featuring a number of characters from the film.

▼ Totoro and Mei

▼ Mei and Satsuki at the bus stop with Totoro

▼ The Catbus

The calendars are made with careful attention to the layout and quality of the paper to ensure ample space for jotting down schedules, and ease of writing with both ballpoint pens and pencils.

All the items in the range can currently be purchased at physical branches of Ghibli specialty retail chain Donguri Kyowakoku and from the Ghibli Museum Store and its online shop (links below).

title: Hikaru Utada sings new song in Shinkansen commercial for Japan’s Supreme Class cabins
description: J-pop superstar brings new meaning to A Room of One’s Own on Japan’s busiest bullet train. These days, the Tokaido Shinkansen has been full of surprises. In June, the train’s operators, Japan Central Railway (JR Central), announced it would be adding private “Supreme Class Cabins” inside the bullet train, which runs between Tokyo and Osaka, […]
content:
J-pop superstar brings new meaning to A Room of One’s Own on Japan’s busiest bullet train.

These days, the Tokaido Shinkansen has been full of surprises. In June, the train’s operators, Japan Central Railway (JR Central), announced it would be adding private “Supreme Class Cabins” inside the bullet train, which runs between Tokyo and Osaka, and then they gave us a way to try them before they became available.

Now, JR Central has given us the biggest surprise of all, with a new commercial starring J-Pop sensation Hikaru Utada. In the clip, Utada can be seen sitting on the Shinkansen, inside a Supreme Class cabin, singing a new song specially written to promote the private rooms.

Called “Intentions”, the song is set to be released in autumn, but fans are getting an early listen with a short snippet being used as the theme song for the “Good Day Express” campaign. This campaign serves to highlight the company’s commitment to creating a “good day” for passengers, by catering to their individual needs with the private rooms.

The lyrics reflect that sentiment, focusing on a sense of independence that Utada says was inspired by Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own. This 1929 essay famously contains the argument by Woolf that a woman must have financial and personal independence, a “room of one’s own”, in order to create freely.

In thinking about Woolf’s ideas, Utada ruminated on what her own “rules for being free” might be, and in the process of composing the song, she came to realise it’s the courage to let go of things in order to protect what needs protecting.

These are deep, thought-provoking ideas that we’ve come to expect and love from Utada, and we get to learn more from the lyrics in the commercial, which start with the words “Jibun dake no heya”, which means “A room of one’s own”.

Although the lyrics are yet to be officially released, what we hear in the video is:

“Jibun dake no heya hitotsu, chiisana uchu ga fukuramu [A room of one’s own, a small universe expands]
Watashi to watashi no dairogu, tokidoki Vajinia Urufu [A dialogue between myself and me, sometimes with Virginia Woolf]
(I came but I’m not gonna stay, I’m good)
Jiyu de aru tame no ruru [The rules for being free]
(Got bills to pay, not gonna wait for you to change)
I used to give you all of my affection
Even when you stopped paying me attention”

The video also comes in a shorter, 30-second version, which includes the same voiceover towards the end: “The Supreme Class debuts on the Shinkansen”.

In the video, Utada can be seen enjoying a sense of freedom in the private space, which allows for the universe within to expand. Another touching nod to Woolf can be seen midway through, when Utada sits by the window, writing in the room just as Woolf might do if she were on the Shinkansen today.

With the commercial set after dark, the Good Day Express is a sentiment that runs even at night, especially for those enjoying private time in the one and two-person cabins that will soon be available to passengers. With reclining seats, dedicated Wi-Fi and controls for the lighting, air conditioning and onboard announcements, the cabins give you more control over your space during the journey, and they’ll be available from 1 October.

title: Tokyo’s Haneda Airport opens new Terminal 1 North Satellite next month
description: Terminal 1 gets its first major expansion since it opened 33 years ago. The summer travel season might be winding down, but there are still big things in store for Tokyo’s Haneda Airport. Next month brings with it the opening of the new Terminal 1 North Satellite, the first large-scale expansion to the terminal since […]
content:
Terminal 1 gets its first major expansion since it opened 33 years ago.

The summer travel season might be winding down, but there are still big things in store for Tokyo’s Haneda Airport. Next month brings with it the opening of the new Terminal 1 North Satellite, the first large-scale expansion to the terminal since its original opening 33 years ago in September of 1993.

This extension attached to the north side of Terminal 1 uses a unique and stylish hybrid design, with its lower section built with a conventional steel frame while the upper floor (the part that that travelers will pass through) makes use of wood from Japanese cedar, oak, and larch trees. The result is bright and inviting, and Haneda Airport says the hallway even evokes the fragrances of a Japanese forest.

The North Satellite will have six fixed boarding bridges, eliminating the need to transfer passengers by bus between the building and their aircraft. These, too, have the woody aesthetic found elsewhere in the new concourse.

The North Satellite will also house a combination cafe/lounge, called the Forest Lounge, for holders of affiliated credit cards such as UV Mastercard and UC Visa. Beverages and dessert items can also be purchased by non-cardholders as takeaway items.

Alternatively, if you’re traveling with young kids who need to burn off some energy rather than rest and recharge, the North Satellite has a play area, with some of its equipment made with materials recycled from plastic drink bottle caps collected at the airport.

Note, though, that since the North Satellite is an extension with no dedicated street entrance of its own, it will take a little more time to walk to its gates than those elsewhere in the terminal. According to Japan Airlines estimates, it’s roughly a 15-minute walk from Terminal 1’s security checkpoints to the end of the new expansion.

There are ways to make the journey a little speedier, though, such as moving walkways and the new model of autonomous mobility device “iino,” which can carry four people and is free to use between the hours of 7 a.m. and 8 p.m.

▼ Yes, even the iino has a woody look to it.

The Terminal 1 North Satellite’s first commercial flights are scheduled for September 1. As Haneda’s Terminal 1 is for domestic routes, you won’t be passing through it on your flight into or out of Japan. However, with many of Japan’s great rail pass deals of yesteryear no longer being offered and several of the country’s bullet train-connected sightseeing spots becoming increasingly congested, there’s never been a better time to explore alternate ways of getting around the country and visiting its less-touristed regions, and domestic air routes can be a great way to do that (especially if it gives you the opportunity to ride the Pokémon Jet Red). Just make sure you check in for your flight early enough to comply with Haneda’s new luggage rules.

title: Foreign travelers arrested in Japan following smash-and-grab robbery in Tokyo shopping mall
description: Robbery took place at luxury wristwatch shopping hotspot for foreign tourists. When international travelers come to Japan, they oftentimes want to cram a lot into their schedule. It’s understandable. Even with the weak yen making Japan travel more affordable than it’s been in decades, it’s still often a long flight to get here, and the […]
content:
Robbery took place at luxury wristwatch shopping hotspot for foreign tourists.

When international travelers come to Japan, they oftentimes want to cram a lot into their schedule. It’s understandable. Even with the weak yen making Japan travel more affordable than it’s been in decades, it’s still often a long flight to get here, and the logistics and scheduling involved mean you might not be back again for a while, so better see and do all you can, right?

That said, we’d strongly advise against the itinerary of two men from Chile who, within the course of a week, landed in Japan, robbed a store in broad daylight, fled halfway across the country, and then got arrested.

On August 21, Chilean nationals Pinya Guzman and Mansano Quesada arrived in Japan on a flight from Sydney. The next day, one of them made an account for an unmanned electric scooter rental network, and on the 23rd, rented a scooter in the vicinity of Tokyo’s Nakano Station, returning it just five minutes later, according to the system’s records. The two men then went to Nakano Broadway, a shopping center just a short walk away.

Nakano Broadway is a very eclectic indoor mall, famous for its selection of subculture and specialty shops. On the upper floors you’ll find stores filled with all sorts of classic anime merchandise and pop culture memorabilia, but the lower floors house a number of second-hand luxury watch stores. In recent years, these watch shops have begun attracting a lot of attention from foreign tourists, thanks to their wide selections of rare and otherwise desirable models, the meticulous care Japanese owners take of their luxury goods prior to selling them, and the favorable-to-foreigners exchange rate that lets travelers scoop up high-quality pieces at much lower prices than they could in their home countries.

During their visit to Nakano Broadway on August 23, the 23-year-old Guzman and 33-year-old Quesada were seen spending time inside a first-floor watch shop called Time Walker, though they didn’t purchase anything, but they did spot some things that they wanted. Two days later, on the 25th, Guzman and Quesada came back to the store, but instead of bringing cash to pay for the watches that had caught their eye, they brought a hammer. With Quesada acting as lookout, Guzman waited for an opportunity, and at roughly 11:50 a.m., he shattered one of the store’s glass showcases. The pair then snatched four watches, worth a combined total of roughly 203 million yen (US$1.28 million), and fled, with one man making his escape on foot and the other hopping on a rented electric scooter. After boarding a train at Nakano Station, Guzman and Quesada briefly returned to their lodgings in Tokyo’s Taito Ward, but then quickly got out of the city.

But while they got out of Tokyo, they did not get away with their crime. Two days later, Guzman and Quesada were in a rented vacation property in Osaka, half-way across the country from Tokyo, when they were paid an unexpected visit by law enforcement officials who had identified and tracked them down after examining security camera footage and placed the pair under arrest.

▼ Officials rolling up on the Osaka property

One of the stolen watches was found in their possession, and Guzman admitted to stealing “only one watch,” saying “I don’t know about the other three.” Quesada was marginally more forthcoming, telling investigators “We dropped the other three watches while we were running away.” It’s yet to be determined whether or not they actually did lose the remaining three pieces, though, as they said that their plan was to sell the watches elsewhere in Japan, then take the money home with them.

▼ Video showing Guzman and Quesada after being transported back to Tokyo and turned over to the Tokyo Metropolitan Police later in the day after being arrested in Osaka

This is a good spot to remember that, while stealing is never advisable, it’s really, really not advisable in Japan, because of how the Japanese legal system works. Japanese laws allow the practice of saitaiho, or “rearresting.” Basically, instead of the combo-meal approach of arresting you for all your related crimes at once, the Japanese police have the option of handling things in an a-la-carte or dim-sum style approach. So after you’ve been arrested for theft, you can then be rearrested, on a later date, for vandalism if you broke a display case to get to the items you stole. Did the store have to shut down for the day to clean up and talk to the police? That could be considered forced obstruction of business, another crime and grounds for another rearrest. Fleeing the scene of a crime? That could be arrest number four.

Arresting someone sequentially like this allows the police to repeatedly reset the number of days a person can be held in custody without a trial. Rearrests like this are typically done with no break in between them, either, with one period of pre-trial incarceration flowing directly into the next. With each arrest allowing the police to hold the individual for up to 23 days, unless someone manages to pull off a single crime in a sort of legal vacuum, they could easily be spending a month-plus in jail before ever going in front of a judge. With high-profile crimes committed by foreigners happening with greater frequency these days, there are growing cries for heavier punishment than the simple, swift deportation that’s been the norm in these kinds of situations until now, and if the Tokyo Metropolitan Police decide they’d like to lock Guzman and Quesada up for several weeks without having to deal with the complications of formally trying and convicting foreign citizens, they’ve got the means to do so.

title: Pizza Hut Japan creates moon-viewing sukiyaki chrysanthemum pizza for tsukimi season
description: Full moon inspires pizzas with a whole lot to love. It was a great day in the history of Japanese food culture when someone cracked an egg into a bowl of noodles and said “Hey, that looks like a full moon!” as it cooked in the heat of the broth. Thus was born tsukimi (“moon-viewing”) […]
content:
Full moon inspires pizzas with a whole lot to love.

It was a great day in the history of Japanese food culture when someone cracked an egg into a bowl of noodles and said “Hey, that looks like a full moon!” as it cooked in the heat of the broth. Thus was born tsukimi (“moon-viewing”) noodles, and because historical milestones can serve as inspiration for great minds of the future, in time Japanese restaurants began to apply the tsukimi concept to hamburgers, and now we have tsukimi pizza too.

With autumn being the traditional time for moon-viewing parties in Japan, Pizza Hut Japan is baking up multiple types of tsukimi pizza. But it wouldn’t make sense to simply put an egg on top of a pie and call it tsukimi, since there’s already a name for pizza with egg, Bismarck pizza, which is something you can find at lots of pizzerias and Italian restaurants in Japan.

So instead, Pizza Hut Japan is giving its tsukimi pizzas additional doses of Japanese appeal, starting with the Sukiyaki Tsukimi Pizza.

This pizza is topped with strips of sukiyaki beef, seasoned with the same sweetly savory sauce used for sukiyaki hot pot. They’re accompanied by a melty egg sauce, and also shungiku, edible chrysanthemum leaves, a high-class green that’s also a common sukiyaki ingredient. Together, they give you a mix of meaty, sweet, creamy, and slightly bitter notes, for a complex but satisfying and hearty pizza.

Arriving alongside the Sukiyaki Tsukimi Pizza is the Terimayo Tsukimi Pizza.

That abbreviation is for “teriyaki mayonnaise,” as both are viable flavor choices in Japan’s casual pizza sphere. The Terimayo Tsukimi features the same egg sauce as its sukiyaki menu-mate, but forgoes the chrysanthemum leaves and goes with teriyaki chicken instead of beef for its protein.

For those having trouble picking between the two, or who are finding themselves wondering about other applications of the tsukimi concept to pizza, Pizza Hut Japan also now has the Sukiyaki Tsukimi no Gochiso 4, or “Sukiyaki Tsukimi Feast 4,” that’s one quarter each of Sukiyaki Tsukimi, Terimayo Tsukimi, Bulgogi Tsukimi, and Kurobuta Pork Tsukimi.

And if you’re intrigued by the idea of full moon-inspired pizza, but not yet ready to go full tsukimi, the Sukiyaki Tsukimi Variety 4 gives you one quadrant each of Sukiyaki Tsukimi, Terimayo Tsukimi, Margherita, and Deluxe Pizza.

Prices vary by size and type, but range from 1,100 to 3,150 yen (US$6.90-US$19.80) for carryout orders and 1,580 to 4,500 yen for delivery. Pizza Hut Japan has gotten into the tsukimi mood early this year, as all four of the above pizzas are available now and will be on sale through November 1.

title: Family Mart reveals new T-shirt uniforms, relaxes hair colour rules for staff… but is it all too casual?
description: There’s a fine line between casual wear and pyjamas. Japan is known for its formalities, especially when it comes to customer service, where neat uniforms and conservative appearances are often considered part of the job. However, as some industries face increasing labour shortages, companies are beginning to relax these conventions in the hopes of attracting […]
content:
There’s a fine line between casual wear and pyjamas.

Japan is known for its formalities, especially when it comes to customer service, where neat uniforms and conservative appearances are often considered part of the job. However, as some industries face increasing labour shortages, companies are beginning to relax these conventions in the hopes of attracting more workers.

That’s what convenience store chain Family Mart is doing right now, with the introduction of casual uniforms and a new grooming policy that removes restrictions on staff hair colour. The changes are all part of the chain’s goal of becoming “the most desirable place to work” among Japan’s convenience stores.

The new uniforms were unveiled on 26 August, with three models showing some of the looks customers can expect to see on their next Family Mart visit. The new dress and grooming rules, collectively known as “Family Mart Coordinate”, are designed to give staff more freedom to express their individuality.

Family Mart is breaking new ground with the initiative, replacing its traditional jacket-style uniform with a T-shirt design, making it the first convenience store chain in Japan to introduce a T-shirt-style staff uniform.

As the first uniform change in 10 years for the chain, the look is markedly more casual, with the top half based on the chain’s popular Convenience Wear “Outer T-shirt”, which has sold more than seven million units. The change was made partly in response to staff requests for something that would be easier to move around in and more casual to wear.

The shirts are made from thick 100-percent cotton fabric and have antibacterial, deodorising properties to help prevent unpleasant smells. The familiar Family Mart colours feature prominently, while the “Staff” lettering uses a more “refined” font intended to retain a sense of professionalism.

The uniforms were designed by Hiromasa Ochiai, creative director of Family Mart’s Convenience Wear range, and will be available to staff in 14 sizes, ranging from XS to 11L, with long-sleeved versions available up to 7L.

The uniform itself isn’t the only thing getting a makeover, because under the new “Family Mart Coordinate” standards, staff will have more freedom over their appearance, including their hair colour and how they choose to style their uniform. Hopefully there’ll be some guidance on styling, though, because pairing the T-shirts with Convenience Wear Easy Pants runs the risk of making the whole outfit look like pyjamas.

The idea is for staff to feel like they can retain their own identity while at work, with the new standards expanding their clothing choices and allowing them to customise their uniforms through layering. They’ll also be able to use a working name written in hiragana or katakana on their name badge.

The chain is also planning a staff-only version of its popular Line Socks in a special colour, giving workers another way to customise their look.

While it’s an admirable move for the chain to shake up some of the traditional norms of the convenience store industry, the new looks have divided opinion online, with locals leaving comments like:

 “The green punk look is a bit too much.”
“The chain will be flooded with complaints.”
“Isn’t it all a bit too casual?”
“I don’t care about hair colour. I care more about their attitude towards customers.”
“There’s an employee with pink hair at the Family Mart near my house, so I’ve always thought it was a free-spirited place.” 
“As long as they do their job and provide good customer service, I don’t mind.”

It can be difficult to please both customers and staff in customer-facing roles, but Family Mart is confident that the new look will be well received. Following the popular response to its Famima flagship, which is also taking the chain in a different direction with its street-cool vibe and uniforms, Family Mart is happy to stand out and do things differently from its competitors.

The changes will take effect on 1 September, when the new uniforms will begin appearing at around 16,500 Family Mart stores across Japan.

title: Anime and Hollywood movies cross over in new Universal Studios Japan merch collection
description: Luffy makes a Jurassic friend at USJ. One of the keys to Universal Studios Japan’s success is that the Osaka theme park is strongly committed to the “Japan” part of its name. So while Tokyo Disneyland has to limit itself to IPs under the Disney umbrella, USJ is free to forge partnerships with whatever Japanese […]
content:
Luffy makes a Jurassic friend at USJ.

One of the keys to Universal Studios Japan’s success is that the Osaka theme park is strongly committed to the “Japan” part of its name. So while Tokyo Disneyland has to limit itself to IPs under the Disney umbrella, USJ is free to forge partnerships with whatever Japanese anime franchises it pleases, many of which have fanbases just as large and passionate as those of the Hollywood movies featured at the park.

With Universal Studios Japan celebrating its 25th anniversary this year, it’s saluting both sides of its theming mix at once with new artwork that pairs two of the most enduringly popular anime series with two of Universal’s biggest live-action hits. First up is One Piece’s Luffy meeting someone who maybe (but only maybe) is as enthusiastically carnivorous as he is, Jurassic Park’s T. rex.

▼ If anyone could overcome the apex-predator dinosaur’s aggressive tendencies and become nakama, it’s Luffy, right?

Or, in contrast to those wild individuals, there’s this allusion to great intellectuals with Detective Conan’s titular sleuth Conan Edogawa and Dr. Agasa cosplaying as Back to the Future’s Marty McFly and Doc Brown.

▼ You could make the argument that, with Conan being stuck in the body of a child, Detective Conan is kind of a quasi-time travel story. Though if we’re being picky, they could also have swapped out the DMC DeLorean for Toru Amuro’s Mazda RX-7.

Both of the illustrations will be adorning new merch, with the One Piece/Jurassic Park design on T-shirts, tote bags, and insulated drink bottles, and the Detective Conan/Back to the Future artwork on shirts and mugs, plus adapted into a figure set.

The whole lineup will be available at the Studio Style shop inside Universal Studios Japan starting September 9, the same day USJ’s Junji Ito horror manga merch goes on sale. And should you find yourself wondering what sort of footwear would go with that Luffy shirt, Nike has an idea.

title: Hobonichi unveils new 2027 planners, diaries and stationery with One Piece, Suica Penguin, Hello Kitty and a must-buy Mini Techo
description: We visit Hobonichi HQ in Tokyo to give you the highlights and our must-buy recommendations for next year’s range. Japan’s globally beloved Hobonichi Techo is back for another year, and the 2027 collection is bigger than ever, with more than 280 new planners and stationery products joining the lineup. content:
We visit Hobonichi HQ in Tokyo to give you the highlights and our must-buy recommendations for next year’s range.

Japan’s globally beloved Hobonichi Techo is back for another year, and the 2027 collection is bigger than ever, with more than 280 new planners and stationery products joining the lineup.

First launched in 2001, Hobonichi Techo – Hobonichi means “almost every day”, while “techo” comes from the Japanese word for planner or diary – has grown from a small collection of planners to include a wide range of scheduling notebooks and related accessories.

▼ The brand’s “Life の Book” (“Book of Life”) tagline captures the ethos of the brand’s products, which can be used for scheduling and crafty journalling.

Image: Press release

Hobonichi products are now an international phenomenon, with English-language versions joining the lineup and fans from over 100 countries and regions full of praise for the user-friendly layouts and beautiful designs.

While the 2027 collection is set to be released from 11 a.m. on 1 September, a press event held last week gave us an early look at the new products, allowing us to get all the details on the new collaborations and stationery items in the range.

Image: Press release

Here are the highlights, along with the items you won’t want to miss when the collection drops, starting with some of the most popular characters.

▼ Puppet Sunsun

This blue six-year-old puppet boy character shot to worldwide fame a few years after it was created in Japan, when it became the “Screaming Blue Thing” meme. He’s now so popular that he’s even getting his first-ever Hobonichi range, appearing on an Original size cover (above), and a larger “Cousin” size (below).

▼ Puppet Sun Sun’s love for bread is depicted in the handy bookmark that slots into the pocket on the front of the cover.

▼ The puppet also graces a series of writing underlays and stickers.

▼ One Piece

Yes, yes, yes to all of these new items, which include plenty of original illustrations and famous lines from the series.

▼ Yes to the covers.

▼ Yes to the hardcover techos.

▼ Yes to the underlays.

▼ Yes to the files.

▼ And yes to the stickers.

▼ Moomin

This is the second year for Moomin to appear in the lineup, and fans of the series will love the sweet mood of the covers, techos, and stationery.

▼ V & A

One of the biggest surprises is the collaboration with London’s Victoria and Albert Museum, which brings the museum’s collection and design heritage to Hobonichi planners and stationery in a beautiful way.

Hobonichi is also teaming up with a number of fashion and lifestyle brands for 2027, with Natal Design making its debut…

… alongside Tanaka Daisuke, who reimagined his jewelled lace-on-velvet handbag design as a techo cover, the largest of which costs 36,300 yen (US$227.82).

Those who want to keep five years worth of appointments and memories in one place can opt for the beautifully packaged Hobonichi 5-Year Planner Gift Set.

▼ The set includes a 5-year diary, stationery items and a beautiful cover for 15,400 yen.

▼ Leather Covers to protect your 5-Year diary are another option.

▼ Some of the most beautiful slimline “Weeks” diaries feature Pickles the Frog, Monchichi, and Kanahei’s Pisuke and Usagi.

▼ Chibi Maruko Chan, and Fujiko・F・Fujio Museum with a design based on “Doraemon Long Stories: Nobita and the Animal Planet“

▼ Sometimes simple is best, and for that we have Colours covers, which feel silky smooth to touch.

Illustrators feature heavily every year, and this year we have Japanese picture-book artist Akiko Miyakoshi joining the lineup for the first time, alongside collaborations with illustrators Yumi Kitagishi and Hiroko Kubota.

▼ Akiko Miyakoshi

▼ Yumi Kitagishi

▼ Hiroko Kubota

▼ Artwork from Leo Lionni’s beloved picture book Frederick adorns a trio of covers in the collection.

▼ Classic Pooh is another top choice for picture book lovers.

▼ After appearing in last year’s lineup, Mother is getting two new designs for 2027.

▼ Some of the most sought-after products in the entire collection feature Suica’s Penguin.

These are very exclusive items as you can only purchase them at Hobonichi’s Tokyo Station store, which is opening in Gransta Tokyo on 16 September.

The penguin will soon be ending its tenure as Suica’s character mascot, so now’s the time to grab these items while you can.

The covers are made with a thick and sturdy canvas material and feature gorgeous nods to the cute penguin on the outside…

▼ …and the inside.

 

▼ If you buy nothing else from the range, we highly recommend this Mini Keychain Hobonichi Techo.

▼ New this year, these keychains are miniature versions of the real thing, being one-tenth the size.

Images: Press release

▼ Priced at 1,320 yen each, there are four 40-page mini notebooks to choose from.

▼ While they’re cute on their own, they become insanely cute when clipped onto a larger cover.


Images: Press release

▼ Rounding out our top selections is a brand new range from Hello Kitty, in her Hobonichi debut.

▼ The covers and notebooks are gorgeous…

▼… as are the files…

▼ …the underlays…

▼ … the “Stappo” standing pouch…

▼ … and the pen case, stickers, sticky notes and stamp.

The “Pochitto 6” stamps are one of our favourite products, as they come with push buttons, allowing you to easily add one inked art, or six, to the pages of your techo.

Another product you should look out for is the Deco Rush, a decorative tape that’s fun to use as you won’t really know what images will appear until you slide the tape along the paper.

▼ Other highlights among the stationery offerings include clever stickers in the “Collect & Collage” collection.

▼ These stickers look beautiful and are practical as well, as they’re designed to hold paper mementos in place.

▼ Simply slot your precious photos, tickets and other paraphernalia into the sticky-backed triangular notches and they’ll be beautifully displayed.

▼ Another clever concept is the “Tsuki no Iro” (“Colour of the Month”) collection.

▼ You may have never noticed, but each month in a Hobonichi techo is coloured differently.

Images: Press release

The Tsuki no Iro collection consists of items that align with these colours, so you can match them to each month with inks, stickers, and handy pockets.

And finally, if you’re like us and love Japanese railways as much you love your Hobonichi Techo, these Railway Maps are a must-buy.

If you made it to the end, congratulations! You are a bona fide Hobonichi Techo fan, and we love you for it. With so many items in the collection, it can be difficult to navigate through it all so we hope we helped you find your favourites. The Hobonichi Techo 2027 range will be available through the official Hobonichi online store, which ships internationally, as well as selected overseas retailers, such as stationery shops and bookstores.

title: Nonstop flights from U.S. to Okinawa return after 54 years, making travel faster than before
description: United Airlines will soon fly nonstop to Japan’s tropical southern islands, with a new direct route to Osaka as well. With overseas interest in Japan booming, airlines around the world are increasingly looking for ways to meet the growing demand for flights to the country. Now, United Airlines is ramping up its service to Japan […]
content:
United Airlines will soon fly nonstop to Japan’s tropical southern islands, with a new direct route to Osaka as well.

With overseas interest in Japan booming, airlines around the world are increasingly looking for ways to meet the growing demand for flights to the country. Now, United Airlines is ramping up its service to Japan by adding a brand new route to Naha Airport, the main gateway to Okinawa, making it the first scheduled nonstop service between the U.S. mainland and Okinawa since the islands were returned to Japanese sovereignty in 1972, following 27 years of U.S. administration after World War II.

▼ A significant development not just for travellers but the history books as well.

The new service will operate on Boeing 777-200ER aircraft, with flights from Naha to San Francisco taking around 11 hours, and those heading from San Francisco to Okinawa taking approximately 13 hours and 15 minutes.

Flights to Okinawa will depart San Francisco at 10:35 a.m. on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays, flying over the International Date Line to arrive in Naha at 3:50 p.m. the following day. The return service will depart Naha at 5:50 p.m. on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays, arriving in San Francisco at 12:50 p.m. the same day. The first scheduled nonstop service will depart San Francisco on March 27, 2027.

▼ Okinawa’s beautiful tropical beaches will soon be closer than ever before.

The new direct flight to Okinawa is an important development for travellers, as there is currently no scheduled nonstop service between this part of Japan and the U.S. mainland – travel from the U.S. today involves flying to an international airport in Asia or on Japan’s mainland and then taking another flight. This new route makes things much easier, not just for visitors looking to experience the tropical beaches in the island chain, but for those wanting to visit family and friends stationed at one of the many U.S. military bases in Okinawa.

In addition to the Okinawa route, United will also be adding a daily nonstop connection between Los Angeles and Osaka’s Kansai International Airport, also from March 27 next year.

▼ Japanese news report announcing the new U.S.-to-Okinawa direct service.

These new flights open up new ways to explore Japan outside of Tokyo, with the direct route to Okinawa being particularly helpful for travellers wanting to experience a less-visited part of the country, while also easing some of the pressure on more crowded mainland destinations.

Currently, Naha’s international nonstop network is concentrated in Asia, with direct services to Taiwan, South Korea, China, Hong Kong, Thailand, Singapore and Malaysia. Singapore is currently the longest nonstop international route from Naha, at about five hours, so the U.S. connection is a major expansion of Naha’s long-haul international network.

Hopefully more airlines will soon follow United’s lead, allowing more visitors from overseas to fly directly to Okinawa in future.

Source: Okinawa Times, Livedoor, OTV via Yahoo! News Japan

title: Japan’s final Penguin Suica train cards have already shipped, and when they’re gone, they’re gone
description: End of the line for JR East’s adorable mascot for its revolutionary train fare payment system. For 25 years, a penguin has been the symbol of convenient train travel in Tokyo and east Japan. In 2001, East Japan Railway Company/JR East revolutionized how commuters and travelers get about when it launched Suica, the country’s first […]
content:
End of the line for JR East’s adorable mascot for its revolutionary train fare payment system.

For 25 years, a penguin has been the symbol of convenient train travel in Tokyo and east Japan. In 2001, East Japan Railway Company/JR East revolutionized how commuters and travelers get about when it launched Suica, the country’s first major prepaid IC card for train fares, and from day one its mascot was the Suica Penguin, appearing right there on the card itself.

Suica caught on very quickly, especially when the system was expanded to let cardholders tap their card not only to pay for JR train rides, but for fares on lines operated by other rail companies and buses, plus purchases at vending machines, restaurants, and stores of all sorts. So for the last quarter-century, many people in Japan have been seeing the Suica Penguin multiple times a day.

Back in November, though, JR East revealed plans to sever ties with the character, and now comes more sad news, as the company has announced that the final cards featuring the Suica penguin have already been produced and shipped. In other words, once JR East stations use their current stocks of penguin Suica cards, that’s the end for them, and no more will be coming.

“Regarding the currently produced Suica cards printed with Suica Penguin illustrations, sales will be concluded once the inventory has been exhausted at each sales point,” says JR East in its statement. “Subsequent Suica cards will bear no [Penguin] illustration.” In addition, the Penguin will be vanishing from Apple Wallet Suica users’ icon and in-app images, though the timing of its erasure hasn’t yet been specified. A similar revision is likely for users of the Mobile Suica app and its on-screen virtual card representation.

▼ So if you like seeing this guy on your phone, now’s probably a good time to take a screen shot to remember him by.

JR East hasn’t said why it’s getting rid of the Suica Penguin, instead glibly framing it as the character “graduating,” borrowing a term from the Japanese idol/show business industry for when someone’s current role is coming to an end. Whatever the reason is, it can’t be a lack of popularity. Suica Penguin merch, such as stationery, hand towels, and plushies, have been consistently popular since the character’s debut, and Suica Penguin imagery regularly plays a role in JR East’s advertising and promotional materials. As further proof of how well-loved the Penguin is, there are a slew of farewell celebrations in the works, including a Suica Penguin fan appreciation event in Tokyo’s Ueno Station scheduled for October 30 to November 4, a special retrospective “Penguin Years” website and video, and commemorative novelty item giveaways for shoppers at branches of Pensta, the Suica Penguin specialty shop chain.

▼ Clearly. JR East is aware of how loved the character is.

▼ “Because you were there.”

It’s not like JR East has suddenly soured on the concept of mascot characters as a whole. In the same announcement for the end of Suica Penguin card production, the company also says “Also, once the baton touch to a new mascot character has been made, the new character is scheduled to appear on the Mobile Suica app and the like.”

Setting aside the unsettling lack of a specific mention of a physical Suica card (which comes one month after a Tokyo subway station installed new ticket gates that don’t accept IC card payment or paper tickets), there are really only two logical theories as to why JR East would be adopting this sort of “It aint broke, so let’s fix it!” strategy. Ditching an already well-known and popular mascot might make sense if the company were going to sign another, preexisting character who’s even more popular, like say, Pikachu, Hello Kitty, or Chiikawa. However, when it comes to picking a permanent-basis pitch-character for Suica, JR probably wouldn’t want one that’s already so strongly associated with another organization that could overshadow the Suica payment service.

▼ Sure, limited-time collaborations like a Pokémon stamp rally or station decorations are cool, but no one is ever going to look at Pikachu and think “Oh, the Suica guy!” until after they’ve thought about Pokémon and a whole bunch of its associated anime and video games first.

That leaves the plan of developing and introducing a completely new character, but the best-case outcome for that, a charismatic and recognizable mascot, would still just put JR East back to where they already are with the Suica Penguin.

Taking all that into consideration, odds are the Suica Penguin is “graduating” due to licensing issues. Though the Japanese public instantly associates the Penguin with Suica and JR, the character wasn’t internally designed. The Penguin was actually created by illustrator Chiharu Sakazaki and debuted in a picture book in 1998, then was licensed by JR East three years later for use as the Suica mascot in a deal that would rocket it to nationwide fame. With JR East intending to expand the bank account-linking functionality of Suica cards in the near future, there could be new aspects to the system that aren’t covered under the previous licensing contract, and perhaps the two parties were unable to negotiate a mutually agreeable contract. Or it could simply be that, with Suica having become such a massive and widely used cashless payment system, JR East believes that any mascot associated with it will represent a lucrative and steady stream of merchandising revenue, and would rather have a character that the company owns outright and doesn’t have to pay licensing fees and royalties for.

But again, whatever the reason, once the current batch of Suica Penguin cards are gone, that’ll be the end of the era, so if you’re a fan, grab one while you can.

Source: JR East via Norimono News via Yahoo! Japan News
