title: Farewell Final Ceremony announced for Tokyo’s life-size Gundam statue, will stream live
description: Full-scale anime robot statue’s time in Tokyo is coming to an end, leading to an unsure future regarding mecha in the capital. We’re sadly down to the final few days for Tokyo’s life-size Gundam statue. Since September of 2017, a 1:1-scale replica of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam anime mecha has been proudly standing in the […]
content:
Full-scale anime robot statue’s time in Tokyo is coming to an end, leading to an unsure future regarding mecha in the capital.

We’re sadly down to the final few days for Tokyo’s life-size Gundam statue. Since September of 2017, a 1:1-scale replica of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam anime mecha has been proudly standing in the plaza outside the entrance to the Diver City shopping center in the city’s Odaiba neighborhood. This past May, though, the announcement was made that the 19.7-meter (64.6-foot) Unicorn Gundam won’t be making it to its ninth birthday, and will be removed at the end of August.

With less than a week left, it’s probably too late to put together a trip to Tokyo if you don’t already have one in your travel plans. That doesn’t mean that you’re going to have to miss out on the farewell festivities, though. On August 29, the Life-size Unicorn Gundam Statue Final Ceremony will be held, and for everyone who can’t make it to Odaiba to say goodbye in person, the event will also stream live on the official Gundam Channel YouTube channel.

The ceremony kicks off at 7:30 p.m. Japan time, and will include a special live performance by Hiroyuki Sawano, soundtrack composer for the Gundam Unicorn anime series and Mobile Suit Gundam Hathaway movies, and vocalist SennaRin, performer of the insert song for Mobile Suit Gundam Hathaway: The Sorcery of Nymph Circe, the most recently released piece of Gundam animation.

▼ Sawano (left) and SennaRin (right)

However, while the “Final Ceremony” is taking place on August 29, that’s not actually the final day for the Unicorn Gundam statue. August 31 is listed as the last day it’ll be on display, suggesting that the dismantling process will start on September 1. At night, the statue cycles through a series of video and light shows every half hour between 7 and 9:30 p.m., and from now through the 31st (excluding August 29), a new Unicorn Gundam Statue-Beyond Possibility program will play at 8 p.m.

The Strict-G Gundam fashion shop inside Diver City will also be selling commemorative T-shirts and mugs starting August 29, which can also be ordered through the Premium Bandai online store from August 28.

▼ The shirts are priced at 5,830 yen (US$37) and the mug 1,980 yen.

This is actually Odaiba’s second time to have to say goodbye to a life-size Gundam, as previously the Diver City entrance plaza was the home of a life-size statue of the RX-78 Gundam from the original 1970s Mobile Suit Gundam anime series. The double-dose of mecha loss, though, could also be a sign of hope. When the Unicorn Gundam Statue was installed, its associated anime, Gundam Unicorn, had aired its last TV episode just one year prior. Now that we’re a decade on from that, it’s possible that rights-holder Bandai wants to build a new life-size Gundam statue that ties in with a more recent part of the Gundam franchise. There’s been no official announcement to that effect, though, and even if Bandai is plotting to build another 1:1-scale mobile suit, there’s no guarantee it’d be placed in Odaiba, which has lost some its tourism luster in recent years.

It’s not clear how late into the night the statue will be visible on its final day. However, the official Gundam website still lists a light/video show on the schedule for 9:30 p.m. on August 31, so it looks like you’ll be able to see the Unicorn Gundam until at least that time.

title: No, Japan’s prime minster did not make friends with a cockroach, despite what you may have heard
description: Some reminders: Japan isn’t always as wacky as foreign media wants to think it is, literal translation can trip non-linguists up, and Osamu Tezuka was a really good manga creator. content:
Some reminders: Japan isn’t always as wacky as foreign media wants to think it is, literal translation can trip non-linguists up, and Osamu Tezuka was a really good manga creator.

The official Twitter account of British newspaper The Telegraph greets visitors with “We speak your mind.” Honestly, that’s a pretty presumptuous statement, and a recent headline from the paper regarding Japanese prime minster Sanae Takaichi suggests that maybe the paper should stick to speaking its own mind, since it pretty grossly misrepresented Takaichi’s way of thinking.

On August 24, The Telegraph published an article with the headline “Japan’s PM: I’m so lonely I befriended a cockroach” and the sub-headline “Leader known for working long hours shares her sense of isolation in social media posts.” That presentation can slot pretty easily with a number of preconceptions readers might have, such as politicians being incapable of forming meaningful human relationships, Japan being a weird country, or even just a collectively low state of mental wellness in the world these days.

Here’s the thing, though. While Takaichi did post about an encounter with a cockroach and the emotional response it triggered in her, it didn’t have anything to do with the prime minister, who’s cultivated an image of being hyper-focused on her job, feeling lonely or isolated. If anything, her reaction came from the opposite sentiment, the idea that all living things are connected.

So rather than cherry pick a few key phrases and knead them into inaccurate clickbait, let’s take a look at Takaichi’s Twitter post from August 22, which formed the basis of The Telegraph’s claim the she’d made friends with a cockroach.

公邸について書きましたので、よく頂くご質問についても、お答えします。

「公邸にはオバケが出るそうですが、もう会いましたか？」

私は、オバケに会ったことは無いのですが、先日までは、ゴキブリに会って叫び声を上げていました。…

— 高市早苗 (@takaichi_sanae) August 22, 2026

As I’ve written about the Prime Minister’s official residence, I’ll answer a question I often get asked: “It seems like the official residence would be haunted, so have you seen any ghosts inside it?”

I haven’t seen any ghosts, but until recently, I’d see cockroaches, and they made me scream. I never encountered cockroaches inside the official residences for members of the Diet [parliament].

After moving into the prime minister’s residence, I’ve made sure to thoroughly sweep under the dining room table, to place food trash in a bin with a sturdy lid, and to wash out plastic containers before recycling them. So when, even after all that, I saw a cockroach scurrying by my feet, it was a shock.

But I’ve loved the Osamu Tezuka manga Phoenix ever since I was a child, and have reread it many times.

Let’s pause here to talk about Phoenix. One of legendary manga creator Osamu Tezuka’s most philosophical works, Phoenix is a sprawling epic centered on the concept of reincarnation, The story takes places over thousands of years, shifting protagonists and genres from ancient historical period pieces to science fiction, but always with ruminations on looking for meaning in life, and the fundamental idea that while individual organisms’ lifespans are limited, they come together in the endless flow of time.

▼ Collected volumes of Phoenix, titled Hi no Tori in Japanese.

Now back to Takaichi’s post.

Phoenix depicts the concept of reincarnation, that lives, even if their forms change, are connected, and this left a deep impression on me as a child.

Because of that, even now, as an adult, I can’t bring myself to kill bugs, including cockroaches.

I thought, “Maybe the cockroaches running around the prime minster’s residence are in the middle of a long string of reincarnations,” so I put up with them, hoping that they’d leave the house on their own, but when I spoke to my secretary about them, he was appalled.

“It’s unsanitary. I’ll take care of them,” he said determinedly, and he carried out “Operation Combat.”

▼ Combat (コンバット) is a popular brand of commercially available roach traps in Japan.

Since then, I haven’t seen any cockroaches. I feel a little reassured, but also a little lonely, and sort of sad…

So as we can see here, at no point does Takaichi say that she “befriended a cockroach.” In fact, she says just the opposite, since screaming and wishing the bugs would get out of her house indicates the opposite of cordial feelings towards them. The Telegraph, claiming to be speaking Takaichi’s mind as “I’m so lonely I befriended a cockroach,” can’t even get the temporal element right, since Takaichi makes no mention of loneliness prior to encountering the creatures.

While we’re on the subject, it’s also worth taking a look at the Japanese word that Takaichi used for “lonely,” sabishii. Yes, the most direct way to translate sabishii into English is “lonely,” but the two words aren’t an exact match. “Lonely” often carries a connotation of being alone or isolated, but sabishii can also be used to describe a feeling where a specific absence is making you feel sad. So, for example, if you’re fortunate enough to have a large circle of loving friends and family, but still feel sad when you think about your dad who passed away, you could say you’re sabishii, but you might not necessarily say you’re “lonely.” In Takaichi’s case, you could translate sabishii as “melancholy,” and it’d also be a valid choice, since she’s talking about a sense of emptiness caused by the cockroaches now being gone, and likely having lost their lives, but not going so far as to say that they were providing critical companionship she otherwise lacks. She may be sabishii, but she’s not saying she feels isolated.

▼ Also, just to be clear, Pop, I’m not saying you’re a cockroach, so please don’t haunt me.

Taking all this into consideration, saying that Takaichi emotionally latched on to a cockroach because she has no human associates that she feels connected to is severely misrepresenting her statement, which was actually meant as an assertion that none of us exist in isolation, and that all of our actions affect others. One can debate whether or not her political policies are consistent with that philosophy, but summarizing her statement as revealing that loneliness has caused her to seek friendship in the insect world is flat-out untrue.

To be fair, in promoting its article through its official Twitter account, the Telegraph did allude to Takaichi’s musings on reincarnation. Of course, it also made sure to plaster “Japan’s PM: I’m so lonely I befriended a cockroach” over a photo of her, as though it were a direct quote, and made sure to use a picture in which she has a pensive, downtrodden, and just basically lonely look on her face.

Japan’s prime minister has revealed an unlikely companion during her long hours at work: a cockroach.

Sanae Takaichi said she felt “a little lonely” after staff removed the insect from her official residence, because she thought it might be part of the cycle of reincarnation.… pic.twitter.com/H5JbrodPM3

— The Telegraph (@Telegraph) August 24, 2026

Hey, I get it. Online media is a tough business, and compelling headlines are crucial in grabbing eyeballs, securing pageviews, and keeping the lights on for any news organization. AI translation tools have also given a whole lot of people way more confidence than they should have when writing about international cultural matters. None of that is an excuse to flip cause and effect or to jettison context in your reporting, though.

Look, Telegraph, Japan has plenty of legitimately weird stuff going on. No one needs you bending the truth to try to make up more.

Source: Twitter/@takaichi_sanae via Shukan Josei Prime via Itai News, Twitter/Telegraph, The Telegraph
